coach_says: Taking back with the queen walks it into a trap: after Bg5 your queen on f6 has no safe square (e7, f5, g6 and d8 are all covered by White's bishops, e5 by the d4 pawn), so you lose it for a knight. Recapture with the g-pawn instead; the doubled pawns are ugly but you keep your queen and your piece. Before recapturing with the queen, ask what attacks it next move and where it would go.

Be3 puts your bishop right in front of Black's d-pawn: after ...d5 the bishop on c4 is hit, and when it moves, ...d4 forks your bishop on e3 and knight on c3, so you lose a piece for a pawn. Before developing a piece, check whether an enemy pawn can advance and attack two pieces at once. Here keep the bishop off e3 for now, for example Ba2 or castling, so ...d5 and ...d4 hit nothing.

With your king still on e1 and your queen on c2, a4 gives Black's b-pawn a free push: ...b3 hits your queen, and because your a-pawn no longer guards b4, the knight jumps ...Nb4 and then ...Nc2+ forks king and rook. When your king is still in the middle, don't loosen the pawns guarding the squares near it. Qd1 or taking on b4 kept control of the queenside instead.
concept: gave the knight b4 and c2
also: pawn push with tempo on the queen

coach_says: Your rook on a1 is loose on the long diagonal, so Black answers Qf4 with ...Qe5, attacking your queen and the rook together, and you have to trade queens. Being a pawn down against a king with broken pawns, the queens are your attacking chances, so a forced trade hurts. First bring the idle rook into play with Rc1: it leaves the diagonal and hits c7, and then ...Qe5 can be met by keeping the queens on.

Your b2 pawn is attacked by the bishop on g7 down the long diagonal, and Ng5 ignores it while also taking the knight off c3 and d2, so after ...Bxb2 Black's bishop can come to c3 and hit your rook on e1. Ng5 itself threatens nothing serious. Before making a move, check what is hanging in your camp; here Bxc7 wins a pawn back straight away, or c3 shuts the diagonal.

You are two pawns down, so you need to create targets and open lines, and g3 does neither: it just weakens your king. Bxa6 bxa6 gives Black three weak, split queenside pawns, and it removes the knight before it can reach c5 and e4. Then c4 opens the position for your rooks against those weaknesses. When you are behind in material, look for exchanges that damage your opponent's pawns.

White's queen and bishop are lined up at h7, and b6 is a slow move that does nothing about it or about White's space. In this structure you should hit the centre at once: ...dxc4 forces Bxc4, which takes the bishop off the h7 diagonal, and ...c5 attacks d4. Next time the opponent builds a pawn chain in front of you, strike at its base before making quiet moves.
also: break the queen and bishop battery

coach_says: You were a pawn up with g4 available: it kicks the f3 knight, the only defender of d4, and then ...Qxd4 comes with check. Bxc3 instead gives up your good bishop and, after bxc3, makes White's d4 pawn solid, while your king is still in the centre facing the open f-file. Look for pawn moves that chase away a defender before you trade pieces off.

Castling long takes your king off e1, the only defender of f2, and puts it behind the queenside pawns you already loosened with b3, where ...Ba3+ is waiting. On top of that, ...e5 opens the c8 bishop onto your queen on g4 with tempo. Before castling, check which squares the king was guarding and whether the new side is safe; here Qh3 or Qg3, out of the bishop's line, kept things balanced.

You gave two pawns for fast development, so every move has to gain time. Ng5 threatens nothing real (f7 is well guarded) and Black just plays ...d6 or castles. The forcing move was e5: it kicks the f6 knight and your knight can come to e4, gaining space and time. In a gambit, prefer moves that attack something and make the opponent react.

Black has a rook on the half-open h-file and a bishop on e6 aiming at h3, and Qa4 takes your queen away from the kingside. Black answers ...Bxh3, and after gxh3 Rxh3+ your king is exposed with no defenders nearby. Bg4 was the move: it trades off the bishop that attacks h3. When the opponent's pieces point at your king, deal with the attacker before going after material on the other wing.

Good move: your queen was attacked by the rook on g5, and Qe2 is the engine's top choice, stepping out of the attack while keeping an eye on e4 and the queenside. You keep your extra material and a comfortable position.

Taking on c3 grabs a pawn, but after Qc2 your knight and h7 are both attacked, so the knight has to go back to e4 and you give the pawn back. It is fine, just a little less useful than developing with ...Bf5, which also keeps your knight strong on e4.

Bd3 is a perfectly good developing move here, practically as good as Be2. Just be aware that after ...e5 your bishop on d3 can block your own d-pawn, so you may need to recapture on d4 with the knight.
Nd5 is a reasonable active move, only slightly less accurate than castling first. With your king still in the centre, getting it castled before starting operations was the tidier choice.
e6 is a normal, solid move. It shuts in your light-squared bishop a little, so ...Nf6 or ...Bf5 first keeps more options, but the difference is small.
The position was already very difficult after the earlier sacrifices, and Bxd2 is about as good as Kxd2 or Nxd2. There is nothing to learn from this particular recapture; the problem came earlier.
Rg5 is the engine's top choice, attacking the queen and swinging the rook towards White's king. In a worse position, active moves like this are what give you chances.
Rd2+ is as good as anything: putting a rook on the second rank with check is natural in a winning endgame. Keep improving your pieces and push your extra pawns.
Your bishop on f4 was attacked by the knight on h5, so it had to move, and Bg5 is fine. Be3 is slightly more solid, but the difference is tiny.
